Place them before the numerals

rules.quote: Write amounts using the relevant currency symbol followed by numerals.
rules.violation_condition: A literal monetary amount lacks numeral-and-currency-marker notation, or its currency marker is on the wrong side of the numerals.
when: Currency symbols precede the numerals.
For amounts below $1, either decimal notation or whole-number cents notation is allowed. In cents notation, ‘c’ follows the numerals.
Currency codes are an alternative to currency symbols.
Former Australian currency units and expressions rather than actual amounts have separate rules requiring words.
Large amounts may combine numerals with a scale word or shortened form.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates currency-marker placement and the cents-form exception into one notation check.

covers.quote: Don’t add a space between the numerals and the ‘c’.
Don’t place a space between the IBAN currency code and the numerals.
don’t insert a space.

rules.quote: Don’t put a space between the currency symbol and the numerals.
rules.violation_condition: Whitespace separates an amount’s numerals from its currency symbol, currency code or cents suffix.
when: Applies to currency symbols before numerals, currency codes before numerals and ‘c’ after numerals.
A parenthetical introduction of a symbol, such as ‘Japanese yen (¥) 901’, is an explanation rather than ordinary symbol-and-amount notation.
rules.why: G-2 combines the symbol, cents and currency-code cases of the same unwanted-spacing check.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop after the ‘c’ unless it’s at the end of a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: The cents suffix ‘c’ is followed by a full stop that is not sentence-ending punctuation.
when: Applies to ‘c’ used as the cents suffix.
A full stop is allowed when it ends the sentence.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the sentence-ending exception within the cents-punctuation check.

covers.quote: If the amount is less than 10 cents, use a zero before the number of cents.

rules.quote: If the amount is a decimal number, always use 2 digits after the decimal point.
rules.violation_condition: A monetary amount written as a decimal has other than 2 digits after the decimal point, including a missing zero before a single-digit number of cents.
when: Applies when an amount is written in decimal notation.
For a decimal amount below 10 cents, the cents portion begins with zero.
Does not require adding a decimal portion to an amount written as a whole number.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 absorb the below-10-cents case because it would otherwise flag the same missing digit twice.

covers.quote: Where content is clearly only referencing Australian dollars, use ‘$’.
If users could be confused about the currency being referenced, place ‘A’ before the ‘$’.

rules.quote: When referencing ‘dollar’ currencies, use a country prefix followed by the ‘$’ symbol – for example, A$, C$, NZ$, US$.
rules.violation_condition: A dollar amount uses an inappropriate country designation: an unqualified ‘$’ for a non-Australian currency or an ambiguous Australian-dollar reference, or an Australian prefix where the content clearly references only Australian dollars.
when: Applies when dollar-symbol notation is used rather than currency codes.
Use bare ‘$’ where the content clearly references only Australian dollars.
Use ‘A$’ where readers could otherwise misunderstand an Australian-dollar reference.
Use a country prefix for non-Australian dollar currencies.
For potentially confusing non-Australian currency references, the page directs writers to use 3-letter currency codes.
rules.why: G-2 combines country-prefix selection and the Australian-dollar exception as conditions of one designation check.

rules.quote: Don’t insert a space between them.
rules.violation_condition: Whitespace separates the ‘A’ from the ‘$’ in an Australian-dollar symbol.
when: Applies to the ‘A$’ Australian-dollar symbol.
rules.why: The spacing inside ‘A$’ is distinct from spacing between a currency marker and its numerals.

covers.quote: Avoid the use of non-Australian currency symbols where possible.
This is the preferred method because it doesn’t use symbols and makes content more accessible.
If there is any chance of confusion, use the 3-letter IBAN codes.
Use the currency symbol only, for example ‘£’ for the British pound, if you have evidence that it is the best way to meet a user need.

rules.quote: Use the 3-letter International Bank Account Number (IBAN) currency codes – for example, THB, USD, VND.
rules.violation_condition: A non-Australian currency reference uses symbol-based notation instead of a feasible 3-letter currency code, particularly where the symbol could cause confusion.
when: The preference applies when referencing non-Australian currencies.
Country-prefixed dollar symbols are a stated alternative.
If a non-Australian dollar reference could be confused, use the 3-letter code.
A currency symbol alone is allowed when there is evidence that it best meets a user need.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4 consolidate the accessible-notation preference, its confusion condition and its permitted alternatives.

rules.quote: Use them for all currencies referenced in the content (including Australian dollars).
rules.violation_condition: Content using IBAN currency codes leaves another referenced currency, including Australian dollars, in symbol or other non-code notation.
when: Applies when IBAN currency-code notation is used in the content.
rules.why: This checks consistent application of the chosen notation, not the separate preference for choosing codes.

rules.quote: Use the same number of decimal places for all the currencies you refer to.
rules.violation_condition: Currencies referenced using IBAN codes are presented with inconsistent numbers of decimal places.
when: Applies under the page’s instructions for using IBAN currency codes.
rules.why: This is a cross-currency consistency check, distinct from checking the format of an individual decimal amount.

covers.quote: The Japanese yen symbol isn’t very widely known in Australia, so explain it at first mention unless you're writing for a specialist audience familiar with the symbol.

rules.quote: Explain them on first use unless they are very widely known (for example, US$).

rules.violation_condition: An unfamiliar foreign currency symbol is first used without explanation, or a very widely known symbol such as US$ receives an unnecessary first-use explanation.
when: Applies when foreign currency symbols are used.

Do not explain very widely known symbols such as US$ at first use.

covers.quote: Don’t use both the currency symbol and the IBAN currency code. This also applies when writing Australian dollar amounts.

rules.quote: Don’t also use the IBAN currency code.

when: Applies to Australian-dollar amounts as well as foreign-currency amounts.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 absorb the example’s restatement and its explicit Australian-dollar scope.

covers.quote: Few people would recognise these symbols now, so write them out in full.

rules.quote: Use words rather than symbols for former Australian currency.

rules.why: G-3 and G-4 retain one words-over-symbols rule with the later disambiguating-symbol exception.

rules.quote: If there is any chance of confusion, state ‘former Australian pounds’ or use the symbol ‘A£’.

when: Applies when readers could confuse former Australian pounds with another country’s pounds.

rules.why: This checks missing currency identification, distinct from the general spelling-out requirement.

covers.quote: Use in descriptive text.
Use in a financial report.

rules.quote: Use the level of precision needed for the content.
